title: Apple Still Working on Giant Foldable iPad That Could Cost $5,000
html:
Apple is still developing a large foldable iPad despite ongoing technical challenges and uncertainty about whether it will ever launch, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Speaking on the latest episode of the "Power On" podcast, Gurman revived discussion about the device, known internally as "Project J312." He described it as a foldable iPad with a display measuring around 19 to 20 inches, saying it would resemble a "gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside." The device could cost between $3,000 and $5,000.

Apple apparently originally wanted to announce the device by 2027, before pushing that target to 2028. The timeframe has since slipped to around 2029, although Gurman cautioned that it remains uncertain whether the product will ever reach the market.

Gurman cited cost and display manufacturing yield issues among the obstacles facing development, along with concerns that the ‌iPad‌ could be cumbersome. Apple has also yet to determine which operating system it would run, with macOS, iPadOS, and an entirely new platform all remaining possibilities. Gurman described the unresolved software direction as another complication, but expressed excitement about the device's potential.

The comments follow a report from research firm Omdia in September, which claimed that Apple had canceled plans for a foldable MacBook measuring between 16.1 and 18 inches when unfolded. Earlier reports had described that device as a large-screened foldable ‌iPad‌, although it remains unclear whether Omdia was referring to the same project Gurman discussed.

Gurman discussed the foldable ‌iPad‌ in April, describing it as a priority for John Ternus while warning that it could remain an unreleased experiment. The potential 2029 timeframe was already part of Gurman's report from October 2025, when weight and display technology issues were said to threaten Apple's earlier 2028 target.
summary: Apple is still developing a large foldable iPad despite ongoing technical challenges and uncertainty about whether it will ever launch, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
